analysis.one_liner: Orders refunds, with interest, of electricity charges regulators find were gouged during the Western power crisis.
analysis.headline: The bill won 35 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2000-2001 Western electricity crisis, wholesale prices spiked and households and businesses paid sharply higher power bills. This bill would have directed the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to order refunds of any charges it found were not just and reasonable for electricity sold in the Western United States between June 1, 2000 and the bill's enactment, with interest paid to the customers who overpaid, and would have let state governments sue in federal court to enforce the refunds. It was introduced in June 2001, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity customers in the Western states — especially California households and businesses — who paid inflated power bills during the 2000-2001 crisis would have received refunds with interest for any charges found unjust and unreasonable. State governments would also have gained a new tool to sue for enforcement on their residents' behalf.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to order refunds of electricity rates and charges that were not just and reasonable on sales in the Western Systems Coordinating Council region, overriding the normal time limits in the Federal Power Act for the crisis period.
Refunds would cover charges paid between June 1, 2000 and the bill's enactment — the heart of the Western price spike — and would be paid with interest to the people who actually paid the rates.
Lets any affected state sue in federal district court to enforce the refunds, so state attorneys general could act even if federal regulators moved slowly.
Won 35 cosponsors in its first weeks, including both California Democrats and two California Republicans (Reps. Issa and Hunter), showing support across party lines in the affected region.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity generators and marketers that sold power into the Western market during the crisis would have had to return any charges regulators found excessive, with interest — money that during the 2000-2001 spike ran into the billions of dollars across the region.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not define what counts as 'unjust and unreasonable,' so the actual refund amounts would depend entirely on FERC's case-by-case findings, making the benefit uncertain for customers.

Retroactively requiring refunds of charges already paid — overriding the Federal Power Act's normal time limits — is legally aggressive, and generators would likely have challenged it in court, delaying or shrinking the relief.

Mandatory refunds with interest could discourage generators from selling into the Western market during a future shortage, an objection utilities and traders would raise, though the bill is limited to the 2000-2001 period.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ratepayers who paid some of the highest electricity prices in the country's history, the bill offered direct, tangible money back with interest, plus state enforcement power. The real costs fall on the generators and traders who sold at those prices, and the main honest objections are uncertainty about how much FERC would actually refund and the legal risk of a retroactive mandate. On balance it was a straightforward consumer-relief bill aimed at one well-documented price spike.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2003 — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on June 21, 2001, joined by 34 original cosponsors from the Western states.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
On July 6, 2001 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, which was the last action the bill ever received.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity generators and marketers kept the crisis-era revenues the bill would have clawed back; ratepayers who overpaid never saw refunds. The committee leadership that never scheduled action paid no price for the inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers kept the money

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 34 original cosponsors, all but two from California.

for.name: 35 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt and two Republicans, Reps. Issa and Hunter.

against.name: W.J. (Billy) Tauzin

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where the bill was sent
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after the July 2001 subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored almost entirely by Democrats (33 of 208 House Democrats) with two Republican cosponsors from California, and the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to refund crisis-era charges regulators found excessive, with interest, hitting sellers who reaped the 2000-2001 price spike — the period when California's wholesale costs rose roughly tenfold. Their gain from the bill dying was keeping that revenue.

Retail utilities that passed wholesale costs to customers would face refund liability only for charges found unjust and unreasonable, and some (like California's strapped utilities) had argued those costs reflected market prices they did not set. The effect depends on the seller, not the customer class.
